nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What was the main focus of the article regarding the COVID-19 pandemic?
nodes.answer: The article aimed to investigate the impact of the COVID-19 lockdown on water, energy, and food accessibility in Katsina state, Nigeria.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract The recent COVID-19 pandemic has considerably impacted negatively on many aspects of human life such as access to basic necessities including water, energy and food. This article aims to investigate the impact of the COVID-19 lockdown on the water, energy and food accessibility in Katsina state, Nigeria. The sur - vey involved the administration of a questionnaire to a total of 900 households out of which 66.7% representing 600 urban households and 33.3% are linked to 300 households of the rural sampled households. The null hypothesis (HO) was that there was no significant influence of the COVID-19 pandemic on the water, energy and food security concerning households. A paired t -test analysed the statistical mean of the water-energy-food accessibility under two scenarios (i.e. pre-COVID-19 and post-COVID-19 lockdown). The investigation found that the lockdown measures introduced to control the spread of COVID-19 had a signif- icant influence on the accessibility of water, energy and food. Results revealed that admission to safely managed water provisions dropped from 30.0 to 24.6% across the scenarios. The electricity index access has also reduced from 1.9 to 1.5.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What has exacerbated the challenges of managing water, energy, and food resources?
nodes.answer: The pandemic has exacerbated the challenges of managing these resources by impacting water and food contamination and causing unemployment, social unrest, and disruptions in supply chains.
nodes.paragraph: Water, energy and food resource management faces challenges such as limited accessibility, increas- ing demand and risks from the international market. Considering an anticipated global population of about 9 billion by 2050, food and energy production are expected to increase by 70% and 50%, respectively, while water demand will increase by 55%. Half of the global population is predicted to experience water stress by 2050 (UNDP, 2015). Limited access to land and water will lead to trade- offs and competition between food and energy production. These challenges have been exacerbated by the pandemic, with directly impacts on both water and food contamination, and indirectly effects unemployment, social unrest and disrup- tions in supply chains. Low- and middle-income states are particularly suscepti- ble to these impacts (Diffenbaugh et al., 2020). Studies highlighted the vulnerabilities and gaps in the existing systems and proposed strategies for enhancing resilience and sustainability in the face of simi- lar future crises (Cheshmehzangi, 2020; Deaton & Deaton, 2020). The pandemic served as a wake-up call for the importance of integrated approaches to address the interdependencies between the water, energy and food segments.
